cues.text: Welcome to Organic Oxygen.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
An alcohol has hydroxyl attached to a saturated carbon; a phenol has hydroxyl
directly on an aromatic ring.
An ether links two carbon groups through oxygen.
An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen, whereas a
ketone has two carbon substituents.
A carboxylic acid contains a carbonyl and hydroxyl at the same carbon.
Classify alcohols by the number of carbon groups attached to the carbon
carrying hydroxyl, not by counting every hydroxyl in the molecule.
Ethanol is primary, isopropyl alcohol secondary and tert butyl alcohol
tertiary.
This classification helps predict oxidation and dehydration, but the reagent
still decides what reaction actually occurs.
Compare ethanol with dimethyl ether: they share a molecular formula but differ
in connectivity and hydrogen bonding.
A carbonyl oxygen does not make a compound an alcohol, and two oxygens do not
automatically make a carboxylic acid.
Trace the bonds around the functional carbon.
An ester has an oxygen bonded to a carbon group in place of the acid's
hydroxyl
hydrogen.
A primary alcohol can oxidize to an aldehyde under suitable controlled
conditions, or further to a carboxylic acid with stronger aqueous oxidation.
A secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
A tertiary alcohol lacks the hydrogen on its hydroxyl bearing carbon needed
for
the usual direct oxidation; harsh oxidation may instead break carbon carbon
bonds.
Acid catalysed dehydration removes water to make an alkene.
Protonating hydroxyl makes water a better leaving group.
Secondary and tertiary substrates can involve carbocations and rearrangement;
do not require a free primary carbocation for every primary alcohol.
Heating ethanol with suitable acid can form ethene, while different
temperatures and conditions can favour ether formation.
For ethanol, controlled oxidation retains both carbons in acetaldehyde.
Further oxidation gives acetic acid without adding another carbon.
Reducing acetone instead gives isopropyl alcohol, the reverse functional group
change of secondary alcohol oxidation.
In dehydration the oxygen leaves as part of water, so oxygen accounting
differs
from oxidation.
Compare products by both atom inventory and functional group rather than by
the
word heating alone.
Phenol is more acidic than an ordinary alcohol because the phenoxide conjugate
base benefits from resonance delocalization.
Carboxylate ions share negative charge over two oxygens and are generally more
stabilized still.
These are comparisons under comparable conditions, not permission to apply one
acidity ranking to every substituted molecule.
Phenol reacts with aqueous hydroxide to form phenoxide but ordinarily does not
release carbon dioxide from bicarbonate as a carboxylic acid does.
Its hydroxyl group activates the ring and directs electrophilic substitution
towards ortho and para sites.
Bromine water can give 2,4,6 tribromophenol; controlled nitration can give
ortho/para products.
Reimer Tiemann formylation gives an ortho hydroxy aldehyde as the usual major
product after work up.
Substituents can change these comparisons.
An electron withdrawing group can stabilize phenoxide and increase phenol
acidity, while its position affects resonance participation.
The phenolic proton is not the same as a hydrogen attached to ring carbon.
In Reimer Tiemann chemistry, a new carbon is added to the ring as part of an
aldehyde group.
Count seven carbons in the usual salicylaldehyde product compared with six in
phenol.
The carbon oxygen double bond is polarized, making carbon electron deficient.
A nucleophile forms a bond to carbon while the pi electron pair moves towards
oxygen, producing a tetrahedral intermediate.
Proton transfer then gives the appropriate product.
Simple aldehydes are often more reactive than comparable ketones because they
have less crowding and less electron donation from alkyl groups.
Cyanide addition followed by protonation gives a cyanohydrin under suitable
conditions.
Hydroxylamine can form an oxime, and suitable ammonia derivatives form other
carbonyl derivatives through addition followed by water loss.
A Grignard reagent adds a carbon group and, after acidic work up, gives an
alcohol.
Acidic protons or moisture can quench it before this addition.
A trigonal planar carbonyl carbon becomes tetrahedral during addition.
If the final carbon has four different substituents, a new stereogenic centre
may result.
Under ordinary achiral conditions, attack on either face can give enantiomeric
products rather than one guaranteed pure stereoisomer.
This geometric consequence is separate from whether an aldehyde reacts faster
than a ketone.
Always inspect the product's four attached groups.
A suitable hydride reduction converts an aldehyde to a primary alcohol and a
ketone to a secondary alcohol.
This retains oxygen as hydroxyl.
Clemmensen reduction under acidic conditions and Wolff Kishner reduction under
basic conditions instead convert a compatible carbonyl group to methylene.
Choose conditions that the other functional groups can tolerate.
Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylic acids or their salts in common
tests; ketones generally resist these mild oxidations.
Tollens' silver mirror response supports an oxidizable substrate, but is not
uniquely diagnostic of every aldehyde: some other reducing compounds respond
too.
Ordinary ketones are usually negative, while alpha hydroxy ketones are an
important exception.
Consider acetone.
Hydride reduction gives isopropyl alcohol with three carbons and oxygen still
present.
Complete carbonyl deoxygenation instead gives propane with three carbons and
no
oxygen in the organic product.
Tollens oxidation is another change: acetaldehyde gives an acetate product
under the basic test conditions.
Acid work up changes the protonation state, so do not confuse a carboxylate
salt with an uncharged acid.
Hydrogen on a carbon adjacent to a carbonyl is an alpha hydrogen.
Removing it with a suitable base produces an enolate stabilized by resonance.
In an aldol addition, this carbon nucleophile attacks another carbonyl
molecule
to form a beta hydroxy carbonyl product.
Dehydration can then give an alpha,beta unsaturated product.
acetaldehyde gives three hydroxybutanal in its simple self aldol addition, and
heating can produce but two enal.
Benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen, so it cannot undergo the same self aldol
route.
With concentrated hydroxide it can undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation,
giving benzoate and benzyl alcohol.
Lack of alpha hydrogen distinguishes the elementary pathways; crossed
reactions
require more careful analysis.
Carbon counting is a strong check.
Two molecules of the two carbon aldehyde combine to give a four carbon aldol
product.
The initial addition retains all the oxygen and hydrogen atoms overall; later
dehydration removes water and introduces a double bond.
In Cannizzaro chemistry, one aldehyde molecule is oxidized while another is
reduced.
It is disproportionation, not a carbon chain doubling reaction.
Methyl ketones contain a methyl carbonyl group and can give yellow iodoform
with iodine and base.
Alcohols oxidizable to that pattern can also respond, as can ethanol through
acetaldehyde.
isopropyl alcohol is positive; one propanol normally is not.
Therefore a positive result does not prove the original sample was already a
ketone.
Do not combine test rules blindly.
acetaldehyde is both an aldehyde and an iodoform positive compound;
benzaldehyde can give Tollens' response but lacks the methyl carbonyl pattern.
Carbonyl derivative formation helps establish a carbonyl group but does not
alone distinguish every aldehyde from every ketone.
Acetone contains a methyl group directly attached to its carbonyl carbon and
is
a standard positive example.
Diethyl ketone lacks that methyl ketone arrangement and is ordinarily
negative.
Compare the carbonyl carbon's immediate neighbours rather than looking for a
methyl group anywhere in the molecule.
Use more than one observation for identification, since one positive response
can correspond to several functional groups or precursors.
Carboxylic acids can release carbon dioxide from bicarbonate, helping
distinguish them from ordinary phenols and alcohols.
Their conjugate bases are resonance stabilized carboxylates.
An electron withdrawing substituent generally stabilizes nearby negative
charge
and increases acidity, with an inductive effect that weakens as the
substituent
becomes more distant.
For comparable aqueous conditions, chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic
acid because chlorine withdraws electron density.
Acid catalysed esterification with an alcohol is reversible, so composition
and
water removal affect yield.
Exam answers should track functional groups, reagent conditions and carbon
count before applying an isolated reaction name.
Chlorine's inductive effect is strongest when it lies near the carboxyl group
and diminishes with separation along the chain.
Replacing a chlorine substituent by a different group requires a fresh
comparison rather than a universal ranking by atom count.
In esterification, an acid and alcohol supply the two carbon portions of the
ester.
Acetic acid plus ethanol gives a four carbon ester and water under suitable
equilibrium conditions.
An ether links two carbon groups through oxygen.
In Williamson synthesis, an alkoxide attacks a suitable alkyl halide by
backside substitution.
A primary electrophile is usually preferred because increasing crowding can
favour elimination rather than the desired substitution.
To prepare ethyl tert butyl ether conceptually, using tert butoxide with an
appropriate ethyl halide is more suitable than asking ethoxide to displace a
leaving group at a tertiary carbon.
The same product formula does not make both proposed routes equally effective.
Strong hydrogen halides can cleave appropriate ethers after oxygen
protonation.
With an aryl methyl ether, cleavage at the methyl side can give methyl halide
and phenol; ordinary backside attack does not simply displace oxygen at an
aromatic carbon.
For anisole with suitable hydrogen iodide conditions, the conceptual products
are phenol and methyl iodide.
Cleavage extent and products depend on substrate, reagent amount and
conditions.
Distinguish ether cleavage from aromatic ring substitution, and check which
carbon oxygen bond actually breaks before drawing the products.
A Grignard reagent contributes a carbon group to a suitable carbonyl compound.
After the addition stage, protonation of the oxygen gives an alcohol.
Keep the carbonyl carbon in the product and attach the incoming group to it.
Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other simple aldehydes give secondary
alcohols, and ketones give tertiary alcohols under suitable conditions.
For methylmagnesium bromide and formaldehyde, one incoming carbon joins one
carbonyl carbon, giving a two carbon primary alcohol after work up.
With acetaldehyde, the same methyl reagent gives a three carbon secondary
alcohol, isopropyl alcohol.
With acetone, it gives a four carbon tertiary alcohol, tert butyl alcohol.
These products demonstrate that alcohol classification depends on the final
carbon carrying oxygen.
A molecule containing an acidic proton can quench the reagent before addition,
so a carboxylic acid cannot be treated like an uncharged ketone in this
prediction.
Identify incompatible groups and the order of addition before using a carbon
counting shortcut.
A reducing agent must be chosen for the actual functional group.
In the ordinary introductory comparison, sodium borohydride reduces aldehydes
and ketones to alcohols.
Formaldehyde gives methanol; acetaldehyde gives ethanol; acetone gives the
secondary alcohol isopropyl alcohol.
The carbonyl carbon remains in the product, so no carbon is added by this
reduction.
A suitable lithium aluminium hydride reduction followed by workup can also
convert a carboxylic acid into a primary alcohol.
Ethanoic acid therefore gives ethanol while retaining its two carbons.
Do not assign this ordinary acid reduction to sodium borohydride merely
because
both reagents contain hydrogen.
Reagent selectivity and the workup are part of the stated transformation.
Reduction of a ketone creates a secondary alcohol, whereas reduction of an
aldehyde other than formaldehyde creates a primary alcohol.
A carbonyl attached to different substituents can also create a new
stereogenic
centre after reduction, so a flat formula alone may not describe all
stereochemical products.
Start with functional class, check reagent scope, then verify the carbon count
and final oxygen bonding.
Chemical tests are useful when their scope and exceptions are understood.
In common introductory examples, aldehydes can reduce Tollens reagent while
ordinary ketones do not.
Some other reducing structures, including suitable alpha hydroxy ketones, can
also respond, so a positive result is not a unique molecular identification.
Two four dinitrophenylhydrazine tests for many aldehyde and ketone carbonyl
groups through derivative formation; it does not by itself distinguish the two
classes.
The iodoform test instead points to a methyl ketone or a structure that can
form the required intermediate under the test conditions.
Ethanol and isopropyl alcohol are familiar positive alcohol examples, whereas
ordinary propyl alcohol is negative in the standard comparison.
A ferric chloride colour response can support a phenolic group but is not a
universal proof of one particular phenol.
Combine observations with the molecular formula and other evidence.
Never infer a complete structure from one colour or precipitate alone.
These are principles for interpreting supplied observations, rather than
instructions for carrying out laboratory tests.
Two named phenol transformations add a carbon but give different functional
groups.
In the standard Reimer Tiemann reaction, phenol with chloroform and aqueous
base followed by the stated workup gives mainly an ortho formyl product.
The familiar product is salicylaldehyde, also called two hydroxybenzaldehyde.
Its new group is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid.
In the Kolbe Schmitt transformation, a phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide
under appropriate conditions and acid workup gives salicylic acid, or two
hydroxybenzoic acid, as the familiar main product.
Here the new carbon belongs to a carboxyl group.
Both products have seven carbons compared with phenol's six, but they differ
in
oxidation level and functional class.
The directing pattern is a useful introductory outcome, not a claim that no
other positional product can ever form.
Keep the reagent source of the added carbon visible in a reaction map.
Chloroform and carbon dioxide are not interchangeable labels.
Identify the new group first, then name the product and count the ring plus
substituent carbons.
Aldol and Cannizzaro questions require inspecting the carbon next to the
carbonyl.
Acetaldehyde has alpha hydrogens and can form an enolate under suitable base
conditions.
Two molecules first give a four carbon hydroxy aldehyde with formula C H
three,
C H with O H, C H two, C H O.
Subsequent dehydration gives the unsaturated aldehyde commonly called
crotonaldehyde, with four carbons still present.
Water loss does not remove a carbon.
Benzaldehyde lacks an alpha hydrogen at its carbonyl substituent, so it does
not undergo that ordinary self aldol pathway.
Under suitable concentrated base conditions, two benzaldehyde molecules can
instead disproportionate through the Cannizzaro reaction.
One becomes benzyl alcohol and the other a benzoate ion.
Each organic product retains seven carbons; the two molecules have not joined
into one fourteen carbon product.
Acid workup converts benzoate to benzoic acid.
State whether the question asks for the initial addition product, the
dehydrated product or the material after workup.
These choices change the formula and functional groups even when the carbon
accounting remains straightforward.
Esterification is reversible, so a catalyst does not guarantee complete
conversion.
Consider an illustrative homogeneous ideal equilibrium model for one mole of
ethanoic acid and one mole of ethanol, initially without ester or water.
The balanced reaction forms one mole each of ethyl ethanoate and water for
every mole of acid consumed.
Let the extent in moles be x.
Remaining acid and alcohol are each one minus x, while ester and water are
each
x.
For a supplied equilibrium constant of four in this ideal ratio model, the
square of x divided by the square of the quantity one minus x equals four.
Take the positive square root to obtain x divided by one minus x equals two.
Solving gives x equal to two thirds, so about sixty six point seven percent of
each starting reactant is converted.
Check that every amount stays nonnegative and the quotient returns four.
Actual mixtures need their appropriate activities and conditions.
A catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium at fixed temperature without
changing
its constant.
Removing a product can alter the equilibrium composition.
